notes.h: The three stages of learning (Fitts and Posner, 1967)
notes.b: A skill (a learned movement or action, such as a shot or a throw) is not mastered all at once. Fitts and Posner (1967) described three stages in order: cognitive, associative, then autonomous. What the performer does, how the movement looks and what the coach should do all change at each stage.
points: Cognitive (beginner) stage: the performer forms a mental picture of the skill, usually from a demonstration, and works out what to do.

Cognitive stage: movements are slow, jerky and inconsistent. Errors are frequent and large and the performer often cannot detect them, because full conscious attention (deliberate thinking) is on the movement.

Cognitive stage coaching: simple, unopposed practice (no defender or opponent), clear demonstrations and frequent, specific feedback from the coach, because the performer cannot yet spot errors alone. Progress is rapid but fragile, meaning it is easily lost.

Associative (intermediate) stage: the basic movement pattern is in place, so movements are smoother and more consistent. Errors are fewer and smaller, and the performer begins to detect some through the feel of the movement (kinaesthetic sense).
Associative stage coaching: add pressure, speed and simple opposition, and make feedback more detailed. Most learners spend the longest time at this stage.
Autonomous (expert) stage: the skill is performed automatically, consistently and fluently with little conscious attention, so attention is free for tactics, opponents and decisions.

Autonomous stage coaching: the performer detects and corrects their own errors. Practice keeps the skill grooved (so well learned it repeats the same way) under competitive conditions, and feedback is fine-tuning.
notes.tip: Do not reverse the stages: cognitive comes first, then associative, then autonomous. Exams ask you to name and outline the three stages, so give for each one what the performer is doing, the errors, the attention and the coaching.

notes.h: One skill at the three stages: the basketball jump shot
notes.b: Exams ask you to describe one named skill at each stage. The basketball jump shot (shooting while jumping) shows how the same skill looks different as the learner improves.
points: Cognitive: the feet are not set, the elbow flares out, the ball is pushed from the chest and the release point varies. The player can shoot only when stationary and unopposed.
Associative: the set-up and release are mostly correct and the success rate rises, but the shot breaks down when a defender closes or the player is tired.
Autonomous: the shot is released quickly and consistently off the dribble (while bouncing the ball) or the catch, under pressure, while the player reads the defence.

Identifying a stage from evidence: an elite athlete winning national titles with a consistent technique is at the autonomous stage. Someone new to a sport who is inconsistent and needs instructions is at the cognitive stage.
notes.tip: To identify a performer's stage, use the evidence given: consistency, errors, attention and level of competition. Exams ask for a stage from case-study evidence and for two ways the performer could improve at that stage, so use the coaching points for that stage.

notes.b: Learners improve faster when the coach gives them the right kind of help. Guidance can be visual, verbal, manual or mechanical, and it works best alongside feedback, mental rehearsal and motivation.
points: Visual guidance and demonstration: accurate demonstrations, video and model performers (someone who performs the skill well) give the learner a clear picture, which matters most at the cognitive stage.
Verbal guidance: short, clear key teaching points, because too much information overloads a beginner.
Manual guidance: physically moving the learner through the movement, such as a coach guiding the arm through a swing.
Mechanical guidance: equipment that supports the learner, such as a float in swimming or a harness on a trampoline.
Manual and mechanical guidance build safety and confidence, but over-use creates dependence and the learner may not develop the feel of the movement.
Feedback after attempts tells the learner what to change. There is more on this in Psychological preparation, which covers the types of feedback.
Mental rehearsal (imagery): imagining performing the skill between physical attempts strengthens the mental picture.
Motivation (the drive to keep trying), clear goals and practice matched to the learner's stage keep learning effective.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to discuss how learning skills effectively benefits performance, and to describe an activity that improves a named skill and say why it is effective. Link each type of guidance to a benefit and, for manual and mechanical guidance, state the over-use problem.

notes.h: Practice methods: how the skill is broken down
notes.b: A coach must decide whether to teach a skill as one piece or in sections. Whole practice, part practice, whole-part-whole and progressive part are the four ways of breaking a skill down.
points: Whole practice: the skill is practised in its entirety. It suits skills that are fast and fluid or cannot easily be broken into parts, such as a golf swing or a javelin throw.

Part practice: one sub-routine (a section of the skill) is practised in isolation, such as the ball toss in a tennis serve. It suits complex serial skills (skills made of several linked parts) and dangerous elements.
Whole-part-whole: the learner tries the whole skill, a weak part is isolated and practised, then the whole skill is performed again.
Progressive part (chaining): the first part is learned, then the second is added, and so on, such as the hop, step and jump of a triple jump.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to explain a practice method for a named skill, for example a method for a javelin thrower and how to apply it. Name the method, say what the performer does and say why it suits that skill.

notes.b: Practice can also be organised by how much rest it includes and by whether conditions stay the same. Massed or distributed is about rest, and fixed or variable is about conditions.
points: Massed practice: continuous practice with little or no rest. It suits simple, closed (predictable, in a stable setting), discrete (a short skill with a clear start and end) skills and motivated, fit, experienced performers, such as repeated basketball free throws.
Distributed practice: practice broken up by rest or other activities. It suits beginners and complex or tiring skills, and lowers fatigue and injury risk.
Fixed practice: the skill repeated in unchanging conditions to groove the movement. It suits closed skills such as a free throw or a penalty kick.

Variable practice: the skill practised in changing situations. It suits open skills (skills where the situation keeps changing) because it builds adaptability, such as passing under different levels of defensive pressure.
The pairs are separate choices: whole or part (how the skill is broken down), massed or distributed (rest), fixed or variable (conditions).
notes.tip: Massed practice is not the same as whole practice: one concerns rest, the other how the skill is broken down. Variable practice best suits open skills; do not recommend fixed practice for open skills except as an early-stage step. Exams ask you to explain massed, part or variable practice for a named skill.

notes.b: Good practice follows a set of principles, which are the rules a coach uses to plan and judge a session. Exam answers use these seven.
points: Specificity: practice reproduces the demands of the competitive situation, including the same skills, speeds, conditions and fatigue, so learning transfers to performance.
Progression: practice moves from simple to complex, unopposed to opposed, slow to game speed and closed to open, raising the demand only when the previous level is secure.
Appropriate distribution: the balance of practice and rest (massed or distributed) suits the learner and the skill.
Variety: different drills and conditions keep motivation high and build adaptability.
Quality of repetitions: correct technique is repeated, not just volume, and practice stops before fatigue breaks down technique.
Clear goals and regular feedback direct each session.
Practice is matched to the individual's stage of learning and ability, is safe and begins with a warm-up.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to outline or identify two or three principles, justify them and show how to use one in a practice session. Use these seven principles, not the list of principles in the 2026 specification, which is not this course.

notes.b: A practice schedule applies the methods and principles to one skill. It plans a single session and then the weeks of work, and every choice is justified.
points: Session structure: warm-up; introduction and demonstration with key teaching points; progressive drills from simple to complex; a conditioned game (a game with rules changed to focus on the skill) or competitive scenario; cool-down; review and reflection.
Over several weeks: set the number of sessions per week and their length, raise the difficulty week by week, choose practice methods and record progress, such as a success rate out of ten attempts.
Justify each choice by the principles and the type of skill: fixed, massed whole practice suits a closed free throw; variable practice suits an open pass.

Illustrative six-week plan for a basketball lay-up (a shot taken close to the basket after running): weeks 1 and 2 standing footwork then one-dribble lay-ups unopposed; weeks 3 and 4 lay-ups from the wing at game speed off either hand.
Weeks 5 and 6 of the same illustrative lay-up plan: lay-ups against a passive then an active defender, with success recorded each session.
notes.tip: When you design a schedule, give the sessions per week, duration, progression of difficulty, the methods chosen and why, and how progress is recorded. Exams ask you to describe an activity to improve a named skill and explain why it is effective.

keyTerms.definition: The beginner stage of learning: forming a mental picture of the skill, with jerky, inconsistent movement and frequent errors.
The intermediate stage: the movement pattern is in place, errors are fewer and some are detected through feel.
The expert stage: the skill is automatic and consistent, leaving attention free for tactics and decisions.
The sense of the body's position and movement, used to feel whether a skill was performed correctly.
Learning from demonstrations, video and model performers.
Instructions and key teaching points given in words.
Physically moving the learner through a movement.
Equipment that supports the learner, such as a float or a harness.
Practising a skill in its entirety.
Practising one sub-routine of a skill in isolation.
Trying the whole skill, practising a weak part, then returning to the whole.
Continuous practice with little or no rest.
Practice broken up by rest or other activities.
Repeating a skill in unchanging conditions to groove the movement.
Practising a skill in changing situations to build adaptability; suits open skills.

questions.prompt: Name and outline the stages of skill learning.
questions.model: 1. Cognitive stage: the beginner forms a mental picture of the skill, usually from a demonstration. Movements are slow, jerky and inconsistent, errors are frequent and large and often not recognised, and full attention is on the movement, so the coach uses simple, unopposed practice and frequent feedback. 2. Associative stage: the basic pattern is in place, movements are smoother and more consistent, errors are fewer and the performer starts to detect them by feel; practice adds pressure, speed and opposition. 3. Autonomous stage: the skill is automatic, consistent and fluent, attention is free for tactics and decisions, and the performer corrects their own errors; practice keeps the skill grooved under competitive conditions.

questions.prompt: Identify three principles of effective practice that could be used in designing skill practice sessions, and justify each.
questions.model: Activity: basketball shooting. 1. Specificity: practice must reproduce the conditions of the game, because learning transfers only as far as practice resembles performance. A player who only shoots unopposed from a standing position will not reproduce the shot with a defender closing out late in a game, so practice must eventually include defenders, movement and fatigue. 2. Progression: the shot is practised close to the basket and unopposed, then from further out, then off the dribble, then against a defender. Raising the demand only when the previous level is secure keeps errors small enough to correct and builds confidence. 3. Quality of repetitions: each shot is taken with correct technique and practice stops when fatigue causes the elbow to flare or the legs to stop driving, because repeating a faulty movement grooves the fault. Recording the success rate out of ten at each stage shows when to progress.

questions.prompt: Explain how variable practice could be used to improve a skill of your choice.
questions.model: Variable practice means practising a skill in changing situations so the performer learns to adapt it. Skill: the hand pass in Gaelic football, an open skill. The player passes to a moving team-mate from different distances and angles, first with a passive defender and then with one or two active defenders who close down at different speeds, and the coach changes the size of the area. Because the passer must read the situation and adjust the weight, direction and timing of each pass, they build a flexible movement pattern and better decisions, which transfer to the changing conditions of a match.
